title: How can a court bring artistic traditions together?
essentialQuestion: How can a court bring artistic traditions together?
learningGoal: Explain how a court's support and its workshops brought artistic traditions together, connect Mughal books and albums with Persian, Central Asian and South Asian histories, and see that a court picture gives a chosen view of a varied society.

evidence.question: Mughal South Asia, sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, with links to Central Asia, Iran and Europe, and an empire whose lands changed across several of today's countries. Look at each whole page, borders included, then at its centre.

sections.heading: A court across today's borders
sections.text:
The Mughal dynasty, a family of rulers, began in 1526 with Babur, a Muslim prince from Central Asia. Across different reigns, Mughal lands included Kabul, Lahore, Agra, Delhi and Bengal. These places are now in Afghanistan, Pakistan, India and Bangladesh. The empire's borders changed over time. This history belongs to a connected South Asia that crossed today's national borders. A court was the ruler's household, with the officials, advisers and workers around him. It was a centre of government, wealth and work for artists.

Akbar, emperor from 1556 to 1605, became an important patron, someone who supports or orders art. His painters included people from Iran, and from Hindu and Muslim communities in South Asia. Together they helped build a Mughal style that kept changing. These labels describe some of the painters' connections. They do not mean that everyone from one religion or region painted in the same way. Artists learned from one another and made choices for particular commissions, or ordered works.
sections.simpler:
The Mughals were a family of rulers. The first was Babur, a Muslim prince from Central Asia. He began to rule in 1526. Mughal lands grew and changed. At different times they included Kabul, Lahore, Agra, Delhi and Bengal. Today these places are in four countries. They are Afghanistan, Pakistan, India and Bangladesh. A court was the ruler's home and the people around him. Officials, advisers and workers were part of it. The court ran the government. It had great wealth. It gave work to artists.

Akbar ruled from 1556 to 1605. He was an important patron. A patron pays for art or asks for it. Some of his painters came from Iran. Others came from Hindu and Muslim groups in South Asia. Together they made a Mughal style that kept changing. But people from one group did not all paint the same way. Artists learned from each other.

sections.heading: Many makers, a powerful patron
sections.text:
The royal House of Books was a library and a workshop together, where specialists made books by hand. Painters worked alongside calligraphers, decorators and bookbinders. Master artists from Iran helped direct the work. In some paintings, one artist planned the composition, others added colour, and specialists painted faces or animals. Akbar also ordered translations into Persian of works in Sanskrit, an ancient South Asian language. They included the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, two famous long poems. These projects connected languages and beliefs. They also displayed the emperor's learning and wealth.

Later patrons valued albums: bound collections of single paintings and examples of beautiful handwriting. The Shah Jahan Album was begun under Akbar's son Jahangir, and more was added under Shah Jahan. This practice linked Mughal collecting with earlier album traditions in Iran and in the Timurid world of Central Asia. An album could place works from different generations on newly decorated pages. Its unity came from collecting, mounting and arranging, as well as from making new pictures.
sections.simpler:
Akbar had a House of Books. It was a library and a workshop. There, experts made books by hand. Painters worked with writers, decorators and people who bound the books. Master artists from Iran led the work. Sometimes one artist planned a picture. Others added colour. Experts painted the faces or animals. Akbar had famous poems put into Persian. They were in Sanskrit, an old South Asian language. Two were the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. These books linked languages and beliefs. They also showed the ruler's learning and wealth.

Later rulers loved albums. An album is a book of chosen paintings and fine writing. The Shah Jahan Album was begun by Jahangir, Akbar's son. Shah Jahan added more to it. Rulers in Iran and Central Asia had made albums before. An album could put old and new works together. New borders were painted around them.

sections.heading: Two pages from one album
sections.text:
In Chitarman's portrait, dated 1627–28, Shah Jahan stands on a terrace. He holds a pendant that contains a small picture of himself. Jewels, patterned clothing and a shining halo around his head stress his rank. Small angels hovering above draw on European pictures. This is a carefully built royal image. Its luxury also stands for the skills of the many makers who supplied the court, including weavers and jewellers. Artistic connections travelled along more than one route and across more than one border.

Another album page surrounds flowing calligraphy, or skilled decorative writing, with plants and grazing animals. Its calligraphy is credited to Mir 'Ali Haravi, who is linked with Herat, now in Afghanistan. The writing dates to about 1535–45; the decoration around it probably belongs to the seventeenth century. Treasuring an older work and giving it a new setting joined artistic histories across time. Both pages show the court's interests and wealth. They do not show every person's life across the empire.
sections.simpler:
Chitarman painted Shah Jahan in 1627–28. The ruler stands on a terrace. He holds a small jewel with his own picture in it. He wears jewels and patterned clothes. A bright circle of light, called a halo, shines around his head. Small angels fly above him. These come from European art. The picture was planned to show his rank. Many makers made his fine things. Weavers made the cloth. Jewellers made the jewels. Ideas came from many places.

Another page has flowing calligraphy. This is beautiful, skilled writing. Plants and grazing animals surround it. The writing is by Mir 'Ali Haravi. He is linked with Herat, now in Afghanistan. The writing is from about 1535 to 1545. The painting around it is probably from the 1600s. So an old work got a new setting. Both pages show what the court liked and could pay for. They do not show the lives of everyone in the empire.

glossary.definition: A ruler's household, with the officials and workers around them.
glossary.example: The Mughal court gave work to painters, writers and jewellers.

glossary.definition: A person or group who pays for or orders an artwork.
glossary.example: Akbar was a patron of many painters.

glossary.definition: A place where skilled makers produce works together.
glossary.example: In Akbar's workshop, several artists could work on one painting.

glossary.definition: A bound book of chosen paintings or pieces of writing.
glossary.example: Both pages come from the Shah Jahan Album.
The calligraphy on the second page is by Mir 'Ali Haravi.

write.prompt: Explain how the court's support brought different kinds of artistic knowledge together. Use one fact about the workshop and one feature or fact from an album page. Two or three sentences are enough.
write.example: In the court's workshop, painters, calligraphers, decorators and bookbinders worked together, and one artist might plan a picture while others added colour. On the album page, Mir 'Ali Haravi's writing from the 1530s was given new painted borders about a hundred years later. This shows that the court's money and interest joined the skills of many people, and even joined work from different times.

speak.partnerTask: With a partner, explain how one album page connects more than one place or time.
speak.independentTask: Say, record or type two short sentences on how one album page connects more than one place or time.

sensitiveNotes: The empire grew and changed through conquest, treaties and government, so artistic exchange didn't happen between equals; working together at court doesn't show religious harmony across the empire or erase conflict and unequal access to patronage. Religious or regional identities aren't fixed styles, and a painter's name alone doesn't show their religion. No learner is asked to share their religion or identity. The V&A article's many violent illustrations aren't used.
educatorNotes: Find Kabul and Lahore as well as Agra and Delhi, and keep historical regions apart from today's countries: the modern names are for finding places, not the empire's own labels. The lesson is about a wealthy court; it doesn't claim to show all South Asian art, all Muslim art or everyday life.

Answer points for Write: connect money, commissions, books, employment or specialists working together with a specific example, such as the older calligraphy in later decoration, the angels drawn from European art in Chitarman's portrait, or the many makers behind court luxury. A list of place names alone isn't enough.

The two pages belong to later album practice: don't call them scenes from Akbar's workshop or pictures for the translated epics. Keep "probably" for the calligraphy page's decoration. The Met credits Nanha on this two-sided page; the later decoration isn't attributed to him specifically, and The Met's record dates the page's two sides about 1535–45 and about 1610–15.

Sources: the V&A's The arts of the Mughal Empire (Babur, the cities, the House of Books and its specialists); The Met's The Art of the Mughals before 1600 (Akbar's dates and his artists' Iranian, Hindu and Muslim connections); John Guy's essay for the National Gallery of Victoria (specialists working together, the Persian translations); Rashmi Viswanathan's The Shah Jahan Album for The Met (how the album was put together). Their judgements ranking styles aren't used.
Both images are complete pages from The Met's records; the portrait shows a sheathed court weapon, and nothing violent. No video has been screened or approved for this lesson.
